overview: This file concerns Japanese military aviation expansion in colonial Taiwan in 1935. It consists of a covering letter from American Consul Edward S. Maney in Taipei to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo and translations of three articles from the Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo reporting the selection of land west of Chiayi for a new bombing aviation regiment. The articles describe competing sites, land acquisition and provincial financial support, planned construction through 1937–1938, the Taiwan Army’s public justification of its choice, and local celebrations and shrine observances marking Chiayi’s selection.

subfiles.title: Maney transmits press reports on the proposed Chiayi aviation field
subfiles.from: Edward S. Maney, American Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The consul forwards translations of three local newspaper reports concerning the selection of a site near Chiayi for a Japanese Army aviation field.
subfiles.summary: Maney reports that the proposed installation would contain hangars, workshops, barracks, and other facilities for an aviation regiment. Because numerous local press notices corroborate the project, he considers the enclosed reports substantially accurate. He nevertheless judges it politically inadvisable for the consulate to make direct inquiries for further information.

subfiles.title: Site west of Chiayi selected for an aviation regiment
subfiles.about: The article reports the informal selection of land west of Chiayi for a Japanese Army bombing aviation regiment and outlines the construction timetable.
subfiles.summary: Military authorities considered sites at Chiayi, Taichung, Tainan, Pingtung, and an OCR-rendered “Kato,” while negotiating land purchases with the Government-General of Taiwan and other authorities. Following inspections and conferences in Tokyo, the area between western Chiayi and Taibao was selected, subject to imperial sanction. Tainan Province was to contribute ¥800,000 for land leveling; construction was projected through 1937, with personnel and equipment organized and the bombing regiment completed in 1938. Hospitals and a gendarmerie station were also planned, although their locations and those of aviation headquarters and the antiaircraft regiment remained undecided.

subfiles.title: Taiwan Army statement on selecting Chiayi
subfiles.doc_type: translated official statement published in a newspaper
subfiles.from: Taiwan Army, published by Taiwan Nichi Nichi Shimpo
subfiles.about: The Taiwan Army thanks communities competing for the aviation regiment and explains its informal selection of Chiayi.
subfiles.summary: The statement praises officials and residents throughout Taiwan for petitioning to host the regiment and offering to bear land and leveling expenses. It says the Army evaluated candidate districts according to strategy, climate, topography, communications, hygiene, and related considerations. After consultation with Tokyo and the Government-General of Taiwan, Chiayi was selected informally, and communities that were not chosen were asked to continue supporting the project in the interests of national defense.

subfiles.title: Chiayi celebrations and shrine homage
subfiles.about: A brief notice announces public celebrations and a shrine visit in gratitude for Chiayi’s selection as the aviation-field site.
subfiles.summary: Officials and residents planned to celebrate the selection on June 26 and to hold a more elaborate celebration later. On June 27, the committee of the League for Obtaining Establishment of the Aviation Regiment was to pay homage at Chiayi Shrine in thanksgiving.
keywords: League for Obtaining Establishment of the Aviation Regiment

interest: The file provides unusually detailed contemporary intelligence on the planning of a major Japanese military aviation installation in colonial Taiwan, including candidate locations, financing, construction phases, and associated support facilities. It is especially useful for showing how strategic decisions were presented publicly as collaborations among the Army, colonial officials, and enthusiastic local communities. The short notice about celebrations and shrine homage also reveals the civic organizations and ritual practices used to associate military expansion with local prestige and imperial patriotism.
